The lockfile now carries Regal SHA256 pins in addition to OPA and Conftest. A PR to the SCP repo that simultaneously (a) modifies scripts/scp-policy-check.lock to register the SHA256 of a malicious Regal binary and (b) adds that binary to vendor/regal/ would pass the required-status-check (the policy rules do not validate lockfile SHA256 correctness) and, in single-operator count=0 mode, requires no human approval. No CODEOWNERS rule routes such a change to @jrnb2024 for attention before it can be merged.

findings.impact: The supply-chain protection introduced by 020H.2 is only as strong as the integrity of scripts/scp-policy-check.lock. Without CODEOWNERS coverage on scripts/**: (1) A PR that changes Regal's sha256 to the hash of a malicious binary and adds the binary under vendor/regal/ can pass the policy-check gate and be merged without a CODEOWNERS-required reviewer being assigned. In multi-maintainer configurations, CODEOWNERS is mechanically enforced — the absence of a scripts/** rule means lockfile changes are never routed to an owning reviewer. (2) The vendor/regal/ fallback path (currently empty, but forward-compat infrastructure per DISPATCH-NOTE §iv) has no protection when the directory is eventually populated. (3) This gap was pre-existing for OPA and Conftest, but it becomes newly material because 020H.2 elevates the lockfile to the Regal supply-chain root-of-trust, which TF-020H3-001 was specifically tracking.

findings.claim: resolve_regal() treats the downloaded asset as a bare binary and has no archive-extraction branch. resolve_conftest() has explicit archive detection ('if [ "${CONFTST_SOURCE##*.}" = "gz" ]'). The lockfile regal block has no archive_sha256 field. If a future Regal release adopts a tarball-shipping shape (as Conftest does), the bare-binary copy will silently write a .tar.gz file to ${BIN_DIR}/regal, and the smoke test ('regal version') will fail with a binary-format error rather than a clear 'wrong asset shape' diagnostic. A routine lockfile version bump would break CI with no indication of why.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 241-253: resolve_regal() — curl download, verify_sha256, return path; no '.gz' branch. Lines 227-239: resolve_conftest() — has 'if [ "${CONFTST_SOURCE##*.}" = "gz" ]' branch before verify. scp-policy-check.lock lines 42-58: regal block has 'asset' and 'sha256' only; conftest block (lines 21-41) has both 'sha256' and 'archive_sha256'. DISPATCH-NOTE §iv: 'Regal ships as a bare binary' — true for v0.40.0 but not guaranteed for future releases.
findings.impact: Failure mode is safe (smoke test catches it; emit_infra_failure blocks CI), but the error message is opaque: the runner logs 'Regal runtime failed its post-download smoke test' with no indication that the asset shape changed. An operator bumping regal from v0.40.0 to a tarball-shipping release would need to diagnose the raw binary format error before realizing the lockfile schema needs an archive_sha256 field and the workflow needs an extraction branch. This is a forward-compat technical debt item, not an immediate security gap.
findings.mitigation: (1) Add a note to the lockfile regal block: comment or README entry stating the absence of archive_sha256 is intentional for bare-binary releases, and must be added if Regal adopts tarball shipping. (2) Add a .gz-branch to resolve_regal() symmetric with resolve_conftest(), or add an explicit check that emits a clear 'Regal asset appears to be an archive; lockfile and resolve_regal() need archive_sha256 + extraction branch' message if the downloaded file begins with the gzip magic bytes. (3) Document in §12.7.13 that a Regal asset-shape change would require both a lockfile schema update and a workflow update.

findings.claim: TOCTOU window between verify_sha256 (inside resolve_regal()) and cp (after function returns): the path stored in REGAL_SOURCE is the location of the verified file, but the cp call happens in a separate execution step after the verification. An attacker with write access to RUNNER_TEMP could substitute the file between the two operations. This is the same pattern used for resolve_opa() and is not a regression introduced by 020H.2.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 241-253: verify_sha256 called inside resolve_regal() on '${RUNNER_TEMP}/${REGAL_ASSET}', path returned via printf. Lines 288-290: 'REGAL_SOURCE=$(resolve_regal); cp ${REGAL_SOURCE} ${BIN_DIR}/regal; chmod +x ${BIN_DIR}/regal'. BIN_DIR is also within RUNNER_TEMP ('${RUNNER_TEMP}/scp-policy/bin'). resolve_opa() at lines 213-225 follows the identical pattern. On GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners, RUNNER_TEMP is set to a runner-private directory (0700 mode, owned by the runner user), making this attack infeasible in the hosted-runner threat model.
findings.impact: Negligible on GitHub-hosted runners where RUNNER_TEMP is 0700. On self-hosted runners with a shared or group-writable temp directory (non-standard configuration), an attacker with local OS access could swap the binary in the TOCTOU window. The smoke test ('regal version') and the pre-existing OPA/Conftest TOCTOU windows provide no additional protection in that scenario either. Systemic risk, not introduced by this slice.
findings.mitigation: Document in §12.7.13 or a security note: 'On self-hosted runners, ensure RUNNER_TEMP is not group-writable. The SHA256 verification window (between verify_sha256 and cp) assumes only the runner user has write access to RUNNER_TEMP.' No code change required — this is the same design as OPA and Conftest.

findings.claim: read_lockfile_field Python helper performs no schema validation on the lockfile beyond KeyError catching. Extra fields (e.g., 'sha256_alt', 'comment') are silently accepted. A lockfile with a structural anomaly (e.g., 'regal' key present but pointing to a non-dict value) would raise a TypeError, not a KeyError, producing an uncaught exception with a Python traceback rather than the 'missing lockfile field: ...' message. The script would still exit non-zero, triggering emit_infra_failure, so the failure mode is safe.
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 154-171: read_lockfile_field — 'payload[tool][platform_key][field]' with 'except KeyError as exc: raise SystemExit(...)'. No 'except TypeError' or schema validation. A JSON like '{"regal": "oops"}' would raise TypeError on '[platform_key]' subscript, which is not caught and would produce a Python traceback on stderr instead of the structured error message. Failure is safe (non-zero exit → emit_infra_failure), but the diagnostic is noisy.
findings.mitigation: Add 'except (KeyError, TypeError) as exc:' to the lockfile read exception handler to ensure a clean error message for structural anomalies. One-line change. Alternatively, validate that payload[tool] and payload[tool][platform_key] are dicts before subscripting.

structured_review.summary: BLOCKED — 2 MAJ findings require resolution before this slice merges. SAFE-001 (MAJ): ADOPT-001 §12.7.13 still declares the Regal SHA256 gap as open (TF-020H3-001 pending); the slice closes the workflow gap but misses the corresponding supply-chain disclosure update, the §12.7.1 pre-deployment warning removal, and the pre-commit hook note correction — a missed closure step that misleads adopters post-merge. SAFE-002 (MAJ): scripts/scp-policy-check.lock and scripts/.tool-versions (the cryptographic root-of-trust for all three supply-chain verifications) are not covered by CODEOWNERS; the lockfile can be modified in a PR that passes the policy-check gate without routing to a CODEOWNERS-required reviewer, undermining the integrity guarantee that 020H.2 is designed to enforce. SAFE-003 (MIN): resolve_regal() has no archive-extraction branch and the lockfile has no archive_sha256 field; if a future Regal release ships as a tarball, the bare-copy fails safely at the smoke test but with an opaque error message and no clear remediation path. SAFE-004 (nit): TOCTOU window between verify_sha256 and cp is theoretical on hosted runners; systemic with OPA/Conftest, not a regression. SAFE-005 (nit): TypeError from structural lockfile anomaly produces a Python traceback rather than the clean error message; fails safely. The core supply-chain closure implementation is correct: verify_sha256 is called inside resolve_regal() before the path is returned, both the download and vendor-fallback paths require verification to pass, and the smoke test provides defense-in-depth against architecture-mismatch false-passes. The Sigstore attestation deferral to TF-007 is documented and consistent with the Conftest pattern. No findings recommend descoping.
